items.text: In this publication, we present Sentence-BERT (SBERT), a modiﬁcation of the pretrained BERT network that use siamese and triplet network structures to derive semantically meaningful sentence embeddings that can be compared using cosine-similarity.
items.why: presents the core method proposed in the paper
items.plain: We introduce Sentence-BERT (SBERT), a modified pretrained BERT model using siamese and triplet networks to create sentence vectors that can be compared with cosine similarity.

items.text: This reduces the effort for ﬁnding the most similar pair from 65 hours with BERT / RoBERTa to about 5 seconds with SBERT, while maintaining the accuracy from BERT.
items.why: states headline runtime reduction while preserving accuracy
items.plain: SBERT reduces sentence-pair comparison time from 65 hours to about 5 seconds without loss of accuracy compared to BERT.

items.text: We evaluate SBERT and SRoBERTa on common STS tasks and transfer learning tasks, where it outperforms other state-of-the-art sentence embeddings methods.1
items.why: summarizes evaluation scope and primary competitive outcome
items.plain: SBERT and SRoBERTa outperform existing sentence vector methods on semantic similarity and transfer learning tasks.

items.text: As we will show, this common practice yields rather bad sentence embeddings, often worse than averaging GloVe embeddings (Pennington et al., 2014).
items.why: highlights the failure mode of standard BERT sentence representations
items.plain: Averaging BERT outputs or using its first token creates low-quality sentence vectors, often performing worse than averaging GloVe word vectors.

items.text: We ﬁne-tune SBERT on NLI data, which creates sentence embeddings that signiﬁcantly outperform other state-of-the-art sentence embedding methods like InferSent (Conneau et al., 2017) and Universal Sentence Encoder (Cer et al., 2018).
items.why: states key fine-tuning approach and main benchmark claims
items.plain: Fine-tuning SBERT on Natural Language Inference data produces sentence vectors that outperform InferSent and Universal Sentence Encoder.

items.text: On seven Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) tasks, SBERT achieves an improvement of 11.7 points compared to InferSent and 5.5 points compared to Universal Sentence Encoder.
items.why: gives headline gain on Semantic Textual Similarity tasks
items.plain: On seven similarity tasks, SBERT improves scores by 11.7 points over InferSent and 5.5 points over Universal Sentence Encoder.

items.text: On SentEval (Conneau and Kiela, 2018), an evaluation toolkit for sentence embeddings, we achieve an improvement of 2.1 and 2.6 points, respectively.
items.why: gives headline gain on SentEval transfer tasks
items.plain: On the SentEval evaluation suite, SBERT improves over InferSent and Universal Sentence Encoder by 2.1 and 2.6 points, respectively.

items.text: This reduces signiﬁcantly the needed training time: SBERT can be tuned in less than 20 minutes, while yielding better results than comparable sentence embedding methods.
items.why: highlights fast fine-tuning time of the proposed approach
items.plain: Fine-tuning pretrained BERT into SBERT takes under 20 minutes while outperforming similar sentence vector methods.

items.text: Using the described siamese network structure and ﬁne-tuning mechanism substantially improves the correlation, outperforming both InferSent and Universal Sentence Encoder substantially.
items.why: reports main result for unsupervised similarity evaluation
items.plain: SBERT's architecture and fine-tuning significantly boost sentence correlation performance over InferSent and Universal Sentence Encoder.

items.text: Even though transfer learning is not the purpose of SBERT, it outperforms other state-of-the-art sentence embeddings methods on this task.
items.why: summarizes key outcome on transfer learning tasks
items.plain: Even though SBERT is not designed for transfer learning, it outperforms other leading sentence vector methods on SentEval.

items.text: We conclude that average BERT embeddings / CLS-token output from BERT return sentence embeddings that are infeasible to be used with cosinesimilarity or with Manhatten / Euclidean distance.
items.why: summarizes main takeaway regarding standard BERT versus SBERT
items.plain: Standard BERT outputs cannot be effectively compared using cosine or distance metrics, whereas SBERT fine-tuning sets a new state of the art.

items.text: There, SBERT with smart batching is about 9% faster than InferSent and about 55% faster than Universal Sentence Encoder.
items.why: reports headline GPU execution speed advantages
items.plain: On GPUs, SBERT with smart batching runs about 9% faster than InferSent and 55% faster than Universal Sentence Encoder.

items.text: We showed that BERT out-of-the-box maps sentences to a vector space that is rather unsuitable to be used with common similarity measures like cosine-similarity.
items.why: states key problem with off-the-shelf BERT vectors
items.plain: Unmodified BERT creates sentence vectors poorly suited for standard similarity metrics like cosine similarity.

items.text: SBERT can be used for tasks which are computationally not feasible to be modeled with BERT.
items.why: states core high-level takeaway of SBERT's value
items.plain: SBERT enables applications that were computationally impossible using standard BERT.
